496: The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302, Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed the convictions but reduced the sentence in each case to one of life imprisonment. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the evidence on record did not establish that the accused or the eye witnesses were present at the time of the occurrence; that the evidence of the three eye witnesses was unreliable because they had been declared hostile and that the evidence regarding the injuries on the accused was not corroborated by medical evidence. Held, that the evidence relating to the assault on Ramchander Shelke was unworthy of credit and the conviction of the appellants must be set aside. The evidence relating to assault on Ram chander could not be rejected merely because he was declared hostile. The evidence regarding the assault on the deceased was not sufficient to prove the presence of the accused at the time and place of the occurrence. The evidence about the assault on his wife and son was not sufficient for the purpose of proving the charge against the accused.
690: The assessee, a private limited company, filed its income tax returns showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49, in Travancore State and under section 32(1) proviso (1) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs. 79,275 from branches situate outside the State of Travancore in British India and other Indian States. The Income Tax Officer determined the assessable income of the assessee to be Rs. 90,947 representing only the profit it made in Travancore State. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing or arising in that State. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court erred in holding that the banking activity of the assessee was one and ind ivisible for purposes of determining the assessable income. [910 D] Under section 32(i)(a) of the Act, the loss must arise in the course of carrying on any business, profession or vocation and not otherwise. The words "any business, profession, vocation or vocation" in section 32(I) are wide enough to include a business which is carried on with a view to earning profits or gains. [911 E F] Abdul Jabar Butt vs State of Jammu Kashmir, ; , followed.
232: The respondent was charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by him in the course of his raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum. He was convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment by the Special Court constituted under section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, but was acquitted by the High Court. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the procedure prescribed by the Code for trial of warrant cases by Magistrates was not discriminatory and violative of article 14 Of the Constitution. The procedure laid down by the Code is not absolute and it can be controlled by the State by making a law which makes a complete code in respect of such trials. It is open to the State Government to make a direction under sub section (1) requiring the Special Court to try any particular case or class of cases according to the procedure laid down in the Code. If the State Government does so, it cannot be said that the procedure laiddown in section 5(1) is arbitrary or unfair.
6728: The petitioners, who were owners of certain lands acquired under the provisions of the Bangalore Act. They filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the acquisition proceedings on the ground that the awards in these cases had not been made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that since the awards have not been made, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. In these two writ petitions, the petitioners obtained interim stay of dispossession therein. On December 16, 1987, two writ petitions were filed by the respective petitioners in the Karnataka High Court challenging their acquisition on the ground of non disclosure of the fact of the awards by the Devision Bench of the High Court. The said petitions were dismissed by a Single Judge of that High Court on November 29, 1988. The petitioners preferred these special leave petitions against the decision of the Single Judge of the High court dated November 29,1988. The petitioners contended that as the awards in question had not been passed within two years from the date of the notification, making the declaration, the entire proceedings had lapsed and they should be set at liberty. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is well settled in law that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with clean hands and suppress any material facts. [823F] 1.2 The petitioners did not disclose to this Court the fact of their passing the awards after the expiry of two years from their publication of the declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisi tion Act. The petitioners did neither disclose to this court that they had knowledge about the award before filing the writ petitions nor disclosed to this Court when the matter was taken up in appeal or in review. [824G H; 825A B] 1.3 The petitioners did make out a case for exercise of equitable jurisdiction under Article 136. The petitioners failed to do so. [826C D]
3019: The petitioner, a discharged officer of the Army, was tried by a court martial for an offence under section 19 of the Army Act read with section 45 of the Army Rules. He was convicted and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 100/ . On appeal, the Central Government confirmed the conviction and sentence. In revision, the High Court set aside the conviction and order of discharge passed by the trial court but maintained the sentence of death passed on him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 19 of the , which is in pari materia with section 19 of Act, provides that when after considering the reports on an officer 's misconduct, the Central Gove rnment is satisfied or the c in cation of the conviction is inexpedient or impracticable, but considers the further retention of the said officer in the service as undesirable, the Central Govt. may dismiss or remove from the service any person subject to this Act. [902 D E] (2) The word "punishment" has been used in the context of the provisions of section 19 of Army Act and the rules made thereunder in the same sense in which it was used in Ch. IV of the Army Rule 14 of the Army rules, 1954. [903 F] (3) The word 'punishment ' in section 19 of , means any one of three kinds: (a) the punishment of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank; (b) the removal from service, (c) the removal form service, (d) the discharge from service, and (e) the award of any pension not exceeding the ordinary rates of pension which would have been admissible on a pension had he survived. [904 A B]

On appeal, the High Court acquitted the accused 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 but confirmed their conviction and the sentence awarded to them under section 120B I.P,.C. The State filed an appeal in this Court for enhancement of the sentence of imprisonment awarded to accused 2,3,4,5,6 and 7. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The charge regarding conspiracy under section 201 is also not sustainable. The evidence against A 1 is not sufficient to convict him. [773F] 5. The charge against A 1 under section 201 IPC is also not valid because it is not proved beyond all reasonable doubt that he was a party to the conspiracy. [774H; 785A]
7130: The appellants are the legal representatives of the original plaintiff in a suit for declaration and injunction filed by the respondents. 6270: The respondent, who was not satisfied with the order of termination of his service as he was not able to continue in service after 30.8.85, filed a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that though he was entitled to be reinstated in service on the pronouncement of the Judgment by the High Court on 24.3.88, he was wrongfully denied the same and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled. [244C] 2. In the circumstances, the High Court was right in declaring that the respondent is entitled to salary till 30.08.1985 and thereafter he shall be deemed to be in service until he completes the age of 58 years. 715: The appellant No. 1 was a bus conductor and the respondent No. I was his sub inspector. On December 13, 1951, the Conciliation Officer wrote to the appellant No. I that the negotiations had failed and that the conciliation proceedings should be terminated when the report under section 12(6) of the Act was received by the appropriate Government. The Chief Presidency Magistrate acquitted all the accused including the appellants and held that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under section 31(1) Of the . The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the object of conciliation is to get a settlement between the parties and the conciliation proceedings would not end in a situation where the conciliation proceedings did not come to an end; (ii) the provisions of section 12(4) of the , are mandatory and they do not override the express provision of section 12; (iii) the provisions contained in section 20(2)(b) of the cannot be invoked against the appellants because the conciliation proceedings have ceased to be legal and valid; and (iv) the termination of the conciliation proceedings was invalid. HELD: (i) The words " pending" in section 12(7) of the are not confined only to cases where the conciliation officer has failed to submit his report within the time prescribed by section 12(3). [864 D E] The intention of the legislature in enacting section 12 is to give effect to the intention of the Legislature and not to defeat it. If the intention of Parliament was to make section 12 retrospective, then there would have been no difficulty. But the legislature did not intend to make section 20(5) inapplicable to conciliation proceedings. [865 H 866 A] The fact that the conciliation officer submitted his report after the expiry of 15 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding did not affect the validity of the said conciliation

1531: The Income tax Officer assessed the amounts received by the heirs and legal representatives of the deceased as a Hindu undivided family. The assessments for the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 were quashed. The High Court held that assessment could not be made on Amarchand and that section 24B had no application to the income received after his death. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "is assessable" in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 24B are used in a wider sense so as to cover all cases of succession including those which come up before the court. The words "income liable to tax under section 23" in sub section (1) indicate that the income is assessable only when it is received by the person who has succeeded him. In the present case the accounts were kept on cash basis. The assessments were therefore quashed. [706 D E] (ii) The fiction created by section 24B was intended to apply to the income which was received by the legal representative after his death and the fiction created by the deeming provision must be limited to the facts found by the fiction. The fiction created is extended to include the amount received by the heir and legal representative after the date of death of the deceased person. The fiction cannot be extended to include cases where the legal representative has died before the assessment order was passed. [707 F G] (iii) The fiction was intended to be applied to cases where the death took place during the previous year and the income was received by his legal representative after he died or by his heirs and legal Representatives after his death but before his death. The fiction was not intended to apply if the income was not assessable in the hands of the legal representative at all. It was intended to operate from a different angle altogether. The fiction did not extend to cases where there was no question of any succession being involved. [708 A B]

It was contended on their behalf that the Act was a Central enactment and it was not applicable to white arsenic, the expanded its provisions and enabled State Government to declare any substance as poison for the purposes of the Act by a notification under the Act or the rules made thereunder. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of the enactment is to regulate the posses sion for sale and the sale, whether wholesale or retail of poisons and the importation of the same. The Act is a Central legislation which has been enacted with a view to regulating the possesse ence for sale and consumption of poisons. Rule 2(x)(2) of the Rules which is in the nature of an amendment to the Rules, makes it clear that the definition of "thinner" contained in Rule 2(v) is inclusive and not exhaustive. [224E F] 2. In the instant case, the Act was amended by the Delhi Poisons Rules, 1926, which came into force from January 26, 1927. Rule 2 (x) (2) provides that the definition shall be deemed always to have been exhaustive. The Act was amended in the year 1951 with effect from January 26. 1950. The Act does not define what are the substances included in the definition. The definition is wide enough to include all substances which come within the definition. [226G H; 227A B] 3. The Act has been declared unconstitutional by this Court in M/s. Southern Petrochemical Industries Co. Ltd. vs State of Kerala & Ors., ; , and M/s Eagle Law Lecturers Association vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1985] Suppl. 1 SCR 657, referred to.

1778: The appellant company was ordered to pay to its workmen wages prescribed by the award. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the wages prescribed by an award could be included in the term of employment under section 2(vi) of the , as amended by Act II of 1960. Held, that the wages prescribed were wages as defined by section 2(v) of the Act and the award did not amount to a contract of employment within the meaning of section 2(iv). The terms of the award did include the wages prescribed under the award but it was not intended that they would continue to govern the relations between the parties till they were replaced by another contract. The unamended definition of wages contained in section 2(V) of the was applicable only to the case of the appellant company and not to its employees. The unAMPIous employer cannot be said to have entered into an agreement with the employee to employ his own labour but he is entitled to make any alteration in the conditions of service of his employee in accordance with the express or implied mandate of the employer. In the present case, the unamended clause (i) of section 2 of the Act clearly applied to the case.

5994: The respondent, a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar was dismissed from serv ice by an order dated 27.4.1969 on the ground of his conduct which led to his conviction in a criminal case. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said dismissal order and the High Court allowed the same holding that the respondent 's removal from service was illegal as he had entered the name of Shri Ashok Kum ar in the pay roll for May 1969 and so far as other eviden ce against him were concerned, it was mostly of acrime nature. Hence this appeal by the Union of India. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal committed an error in not considering the adequacy of penalty awarded to the respondent. [272D] 1.2 In view of the fact that the respondent had entered the services of the State Government in the year 1962, the question of imposing any penalty would be irrelevant. [273E] 1.3 The Tribunal has erred in holding that the punishment imposed upon the respondent is disproportionate to the gravity of the offence committed by him. [275F] 1.4 The Tribunal has failed to take into consideration the fact that in the past, there had been no disciplinary proceedings pending against the respondent. The respondent had been punished twice for the same offence and once again for the same incident. The respondent has been punished twice with stoppage of five increments without cumulative effect. [276G H; 277A B] 1.5 The Tribunal has miserably failed to take note of the fact t hat the respondent had been convicted in a criminal trial. The respondent having already been acquitted in the criminal case, the Tribunal ought to have considered the desirability of continuing the respondent in service. [278C D] 1.6 The Tribunal has also overlooked the fact that there was no adverse entry against the respondent in the confidential report for the year 1965 1966. The respondent was only a pe rson in the cadre of Lower Division Clerk. There was no adverse remark against him. The respondent could not be continued in service merely because he was found guilty in the departmental enquiry. [279H; 280B C] 1
6118: The petitioners are carpenters, 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation. They have been working in different capaci ty such as cricketing, music etc. The Corporation has adopted the minimum wages payable to the regular employees as prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The petitioners are also being paid the same wages as are paid to the regular workers. The petitioners seek regularisation of their services with the benefits of the 5th Pay Commission. The Corporation contested the petition on the ground that the unit where the petitioners are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. It was contended that the unit wherein the petitioners are employed is a factory and not a factory registered Under the Factories Act, and therefore, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. A reference was made to the Labour Court. The Labour Court held that the petitioners were entitled to be treated as industrial workmen and they were given all benefits due to them under the various labour legislations. The Corporation filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed the same holding that the principle of "equal pay for equal work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Hence this special leave petition. Allowing the petition, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The petitioners cannot claim the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution. [5B] 1.2. The petitioners do not fall within any of the categories specified in sub clause (b) of clause (2) of Article V of the Constitution but fall under sub clause (c) of cl. (22 ). The classification of employees into those who are paid from out of the Fund of the Corporation and those who are not is arbitrary. The classification has been made in order to achieve the object. Therefore, it is not only when the fund is created for the purpose of meeting fixed or portion of the pay of the staff, but also to serve the public. The classification may be justified on some 'similar grounds. But, if there is a reasonable nexus between the classification and the objects sought to be achieved, the law will not be struck down as violative of Article 14. [6E F] 1.3. The petitioners
660: The appellant, the adopted son of a Hindu, executed a will on August 22, 1945, in his favour. After the death of his father, the respondent filed a suit for possession against the appellant claiming a declaration that the said will was not genuine and valid and that he was entitled to dispose of the properties by a will. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it and held that the will set up by the appellant was not genuine. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that the will was not proved to be the last will of the testator. [864 D] (ii) It is well settled that if a will is found to be a forged one, its validity can be challenged by any person who has made the same. If the propounder of the will does not prove the genuineness of the will, the onus shifts on to the party who disputes the validity of the document to show that the document is invalid. If the party shows that the genuineness of a document is open to serious doubt, the onus could be shifted to the other party to establish the genuineness of such document. If the genuineness of another document is doubted then the matter must necessarily be remitted back to the court with a direction to decide the question whether the document set up by it is genuine or not. [865 H; 866 A B]. (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that even if the will set out the alleged signature of the testator, namely, the appellant, was not genuine, the evidence adduced by the parties showed that the testator had signed the will as a witness and that the signature of the appellant on the will was that of the testator and not of the testator himself. [867 C]. In the present case, the High Court was right in holding, that the execution of the will was admitted by the appellant and that the testator was not in a sound and disposing state of mind. [868 E].
4938: The appellant, a money lender, carried on business as a money lenders. He was granted a license to carry on the business of selling and distributing ornaments in the region called the Golden Handshake area under section 28(1)(a) of the . In exercise of his power under section 27(6) of the , he renewed the license for a period of five years with effect from 1st April, 1973. The appellant 's application for renewal was rejected by the Administrator on the ground that the licensing authority had no power to renew the license after the expiry of its term. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order rejecting his application for renewal. The High Court struck down the provision in section 27(4) of the Act as being arbitrary and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (Per Krishna Iyer & Chinnappa Reddy JJ.) The object underlying section 28 is to ensure that the Administrator does not act arbitrarily in granting or refusing to grant permission to carry on any trade or business. The power conferred on the Administrator is an uncontrolled power coupled with an unreasonable restriction and must be exercised within well defined limits. [732B] The power conferred upon the Administrator under section 27 (6) of Act is not absolute but has to be exercised judicially, reasonably, capriciously, and having regard to the relevant factors. It is open to the Administrator to refuse permission to carrying on trade or business if the applicant satisfies the conditions laid down in cls. (a), (b) and (c) of sub section (2) of section 27. But the power conferred by section 27(5) is subject to the restrictions which may be imposed by the Administrator under the proviso to section 27(3). Therefore, the power conferred on him under section 27 is subject to two limitations, namely, (i) it must be exercised with due regard to the availability of other provisions of the Act conferring such powers; and (ii) it must also be exercised in respect of one of the matters enumerated in the said clause. [733C D, F G] Harakchand Banthia vs State of Punjab, ; , followed.
5707: The appellant company, which was engaged in the production of newspaper establishments, published a law report on the working journalism of the newspaper industry. The said law report contained certain recommendations made by the Wage Board constituted under section 9 of the Act and the Central Government accepted them. The Wage Board recommended that the newspaper industry should be closed down and the employees engaged therein should be paid wages at a uniform rate of Rs. 100/ per day. The Central Government also approved the recommendations of the Wage Board. The Central Labour Commissioner submitted his report to the Central Government recommending that the newspaper establishment should be closed permanently. 1789: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. 2609: The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. HELD: (i) The rule is not ultra vires the rule making power conferred by section 3 of the Act. [121 F] (ii)The rule is not an exception to the ordinary law but is a measure of administrative convenience and policy. It is open to the legislature to provide by law for the transfer of a person from one state to another or to provide for the creation and abolition of posts in all its departments. But then the object of the rule is to transfer

1378: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He was also charged with the murder of his wife. The prosecution case was that on the night between June 14, 1960, the appellant had a bath in the canal and had a bath there. At about mid night he went to the Canal and informed the Police Station. The Police Station was at a distance of about 100 yards from the village. The Police Officer who recorded the First Information Report did not inform the Police Station immediately but only after the Police Officer had reached the place of occurrence he lodged the First Information report. The evidence showed that the Police Officer did not inform him about the murder and that he had made an extra judicial confession before him. The High Court rejected the statement of Ujagar Singh regarding the motive and the purchase of the sword and held that it was unsafe to rely upon the evidence of this witness because he had no axe to grind against the appellant. It further held that the evidence of the Police Officer was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai or not. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the evidence relating to motive was sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellant. The evidence relating to the motive was sufficient for sustaining the conviction of the appellant and the High Court erred in rejecting the statement of the appellant regarding the motive. The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating the discovery of bloodstained clothes at the instance of the appellant which were not admissible in evidence. The evidence of the Doctor who conducted the postmortem examination could not be treated as substantive evidence as it was not proved that the injury No. 1 which was found on the person of the deceased was fatal. The evidence regarding the recovery of the swords and the dhoti from the house of the appellant was inadmissible in evidence.
4071: The appellants, who were the unsuccessful candidates from the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the State of Madhya Pradesh, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh challenging the validity of the electoral roll on various grounds. 3168: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1950 under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had a share capital of Rs. 100 and its shares were held by it as directors. In 1956, the company filed a return for the assessment years 1957 58 to 1960 61 showing an income of Rs. 1,04,750 and odd for the year ending 31st March 1960. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required by section 220(1) of the Act read with Rule 3 of the Rules made thereunder showed that the company had not only failed to call a general meeting but also committed breach of the provisions of the Act. The appellant contended that the company was liable to be prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) of the Companies Act, since the annual general meeting of the company was not called within the period prescribed by the rules. The High Court rejected this contention. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The expression "any default" in section 220(2)(b) of the , means failure to comply with the requirements of law or failure to comply wholly with the requirements which lay down the time limit within which the company is to be wound up. If there are no such defaults then the company cannot be proceeded against under section 134 of the Companies act. [864 C] (ii) The words "any default", in section 131(2)(a), must mean failure to comply strictly with the requirements laid down in section 220. If there is any default on the part of the company, the company cannot escape liability under section 134. [865 D] (iii) The word "shall" in section 132(4) refers to the mandatory requirement of the rules framed under section 132(2). The requirement of the rule is that the company should have been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause why the proposed action should not be taken. This requirement has to be read along with the other provisions of the Companies Acts. [866 E F]
4568: The appellant, a Professor in the Department of Radiotherapy, was appointed as a Specialist Grade II in a teaching hospital belonging to the Central Health Service. He was later promoted as Professor of Radiology and then as Professor of Medicine. In 1966, he was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview for the post of Professor of Radio Medical College. The appellant was not only holding the post of Radiologist in the said college but also was associated with teaching the under graduate and post graduate students as an Associate Professor of RHSMI. The appellant 's case was that he had been working as a specialist Grade II since 1968 and was eligible for appointment or promotion as Professor or Associate Professor of the concerned speciality. The appellant contended that the post of Specialist Grade I fell vacant in 1973 because of the retirement of one Dr. P.C. Jain on September 30, 1972 and that the retirement of Dr. Jain was due to be made effective from September 9, 1966. The appellant further contended that the retirement was effected from September 9. 1966 when Dr. Jain became entitled to be considered for promotion as Professor of the said specialty. The appellant also contended that the rules relating to the age limit for entry into service were not amended till the year 1967. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not entitled to the relief prayed for. [26F] 2.1 Rule 5(2) of the Central Health Services Rules, 1963 provides that a person who has held any post specified in Item (i) to (v) of the Schedule to the Act shall retire on attaining the age of sixty years. The proviso thereto requires that such person shall not be retained in service after 58 years. The appellant does not fall within the said category. [27B C] 2.2 The appellant was senior to the respondent No. 1 in the cadre of Professors in the Central Health service. The appellant did not even possess the requisite qualification for being appointed as Professor of Microbiology
2440: The appellant company was in the business of manufacturing paper on a very large scale. It had a factory at Jamshedpur in Bihar where minimum wages were higher than the minimum wage fixed for the workmen employed by it. In respect of some of these matters, the Tribunal found that there were other industries in the region where minimum wages could be paid and therefore, directed the Company to pay the minimum wages to the workmen concerned according to the minimum wages fixed by the Tribunal. The Company challenged this order before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Tribunal had not followed the principle laid down by this Court in the case of French Motor Car Co. (1) and that the Tribunal committed an error inasmuch as, in making the calculation, the Tribunal only tried to neutralise about 36 per cent of the cost of living, which could have been done when fixing the minimum wage for the Company on the basis of the alternative calculation made by the Tribunal, and allowed the claim of the workmen. Held, that the Tribunal has not followed the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the cases of French Industrial Workers ' Union vs Their Workmen, , and French Motor car Co. (India) Ltd. vs Their Workmen; , and that the award of the Tribunal is bad because it did not take into consideration the minimum wage prevailing in the industry in the region with which it was dealing. Held also, that the award is not sustainable because, in the present case, the Tribunal has proceeded on the assumption that the minimum wage is being fixed for the Company for the purpose of fixation of the minimum wage. The Tribunal has not given any reasons for accepting the figures arrived at by the two parties. The Tribunal should have taken into account the actual income from the various sources available to the employer and then determined the minimum wage payable by the employer.
2913: The assessee, a private limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61 in respect of its income from certain sources. During the relevant accounting year, the assessee submitted its income tax return, but before the Income Tax Officer could issue notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, he issued a notice under section 147(2) of the Act on June 3, 1966. The notice was then served on the assessee on July 6, 1966. In that statement it gave the lull names and address of the alleged creditors. After enquiry, the assessee 's total income was assessed at Rs. 69,886/ . On June 3,1966, the 1st respondent (Income Tax Officer Ward 'A '), Muzaffarpur, issued a notice to the assessee under section 148(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The assessee filed its income tax returns, but the Income Tax officer did not issue any notice to them till the end of the year 1966. The assessee 's case was that the notices were invalid because they had been issued without giving an opportunity to the assessee to explain its case. The Income Tax Officer held that the notices had been issued after obtaining the satisfaction of the Commissioner of Income Tax, Bihar and Orissa, Patna. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. The Tribunal, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee. The High Court dismissed the assessee ' s appeal. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 148(3) of the Indian Income Tax Act provides that before issuing a notice under that section, the Income Tax Offi cer must have reason to believe that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment within the meaning of section 147. The expression "reason to believe" is of the widest amplitude and includes even if there be some evidence or discovery which prima facie make out a case of escapement of income, the Income tax Officer may take into consideration the information as is available with him in the course of his investigation. [446F G] 2. The object of section 148 is to enable the Income tax Officers to gather evidence sufficient to warrant the belief in question. It does not say that the Income tax Authorities should record reasons for their belief
1697: The appellant, a limited company carrying on business as partners of a firm, carried on the business in partnership with another firm. In the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1948 49, the Income tax Officer held that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that the change made by the deed of partition between the partners was a mere change in the constitution of the firm and did not amount to a transfer of assets within the meaning of section 2(6A)(c) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this view. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the change in the nature of the business was a mere alteration of the constitution of a firm and did no more than an alteration of the business itself and that it was not a transfer of any property or asset within the meaning Of section 2(7) of the Income tax Act. Held, that the change could not be regarded as a transfer of the assets of the business but only as a change in the composition of the firm. The fact that the business was continued even after the partition would not make the change a mere change of the constitution. The change in the character of the business must be such that it cannot be said to have been discontinued before it is so treated. The change could not therefore be regarded as having been made without the permission of the assessee.
5364: The respondent, an employee of the Life Insurance Corporation of India, was appointed to the service of the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. He was transferred from the said Corporation to the Corporation in May, 1957. On completion of 58 years of age he retired on completion of 58 year 's age. In the meantime, the Act was amended by the Act of 1977 which provided for vesting of the management of the life insurance business in the Corporation. The Corporation filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Act is a beneficent legislation intended to protect the interest of the employees who are required to retire on completing 58 years of service but the Corporation has not chosen to exercise its option under section 11(2)(b) of the Act to make any such provision. [732C] (2) The Act provides for the vesting of the Corporation in the Corporation and the same is a beneficial piece of social welfare legislation. 3542: The appellants were members of the Bar Association. They filed a writ petition in the High Court for their removal from the membership of the Bar Council of India on the ground that they had been guilty of criminal contempt. The High Court dismissed the petition and directed the appellants to restore the letter written by them to the President of India. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the letter did not bear any foundation for an action for criminal contempt. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) It is well settled that the court cannot go behind the decision of the executive or even the Legislature. [732C] (2) The principle of constructive res judicata is founded on two basic principles : firstly, public policy and second, law will not enforce its fundamental rights under article 32 of the Constitution; secondly, the court will not enforce any personal opinion against any person. Therefore, the letter written to the President does not constitute contempt of court. [733D E]

2207: The respondent was a dealer in goods carrying on business as a dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. He purchased certain goods from a registered dealer and sold them to others. The Sales tax authorities recovered arrears of sales tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the business. The respondent filed an appeal before the Board of Revenue but the appeals were dismissed. The respondent then moved the High Court by way of a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the State Government had authority under its rule making power conferred on it by section 19(1) and (2) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. The appellant contended that the State was not competent to create a statutory fiction by which a person who is not a citizen could be made liable for payment of sales tax on his own account and that the respondent was not liable to pay sales tax on the sale effected by him with effect from the date of transfer of the business under Rule 21 A of the Rules framed under the Act. Held: (i) The State Government has no authority under its Rule making power conferred upon it by section19 of the Act empowering it to create a fiction by which an assessee who is not an individual but a member of the Hindu undivided family or a company may be deemed to be a dealer under section 3(1)(b) of the Madras General Sale Tax Act, 1930. (ii)The State Government has authority under its rules to create a valid legal fiction by prescribing a fresh period of limitation within which the tax should be paid and by prescribing a new period of limitation for the purpose of recovery of the amount due under a notice of demand issued under section 9 of the Act. (iii)The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., Ltd., , approved.
1195: The appellants granted a lease of coal and coal mining rights in respect of certain land to one Jugal Kishore Lal. Jugal Kishori Lal, the predecessor in interest of the respondents, was in possession of the land on August 2, 1940. On August 18, 1941, Jugal Kheta had been granted a lease for a period of 30 years in respect of the said land. In the lease deed it was stated that the lease would be terminable by six months ' notice on either side. Jugl Kishore Lal died in 1943 leaving behind him his widow and two sons. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants claiming that the leasehold right of the coal and coal mines in the leased area was not an accretion to their ownership but was only a accession to the ownership of the appellants. The appellants contended that the lease was not an indivisible one and that the respondents were entitled to remain in possession of their respective shares of the lease hold property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had failed to prove that they had acquired any right to the coal and the land in dispute. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the onus of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents lay on the appellants and that the courts below had wrongly assumed the initial burden of proving the existence of the first burden of proof. HELD: (i) It is well settled that the onus probandi lies in every case upon prosecution in order to succeed. But where there are no such pleas crop up on evidence the mere fact of the defendants having admitted the existence of a fact cannot be used as a conclusive proof. [864 H] In the present case, the High Court held that the onus was on the appellants to prove that the initial burden which lay on them was discharged by showing that they had knowledge of the existence of their right to the mine and the further fact that the respondents had failed to adduce any evidence to show that they had notice of the existence or non existence of the right. [865 A B] (ii)The High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show when the respondents had knowledge of their existence
1406: The appellant was a workman of the respondent. He was dismissed from service under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders of the respondent company. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the action taken by the employer under r.18(a) was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power given to him under r. 8(a). Held, that the enquiry was not vitiated on account of mala fides or colourable exercise or colourable device having been adopted by the management. The enquiry was not held according to any rules but according to principles of natural justice which have been violated. The enquiry officer had no jurisdiction to hold the enquiry as he was not an arbitrator appointed by the Government. The enquiry proceedings were conducted in violation of the principles of natural Justice and the punishment imposed was disproportionate to the misconduct alleged. The enquiry report showed that the charges against the appellant were proved and the punishment was adequate. The enquiry did not suffer from any legal infirmity. The Labour Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction under section 7 of the , to interfere with the order of dismissal passed by the management and it was not open to the Labour Appellate Tribunal to substitute its own view as if another tribunal sitting in appeal over the decision of the management.

3924: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted him under section 302, I.P,.C. and awarded sentence of imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the view taken by the High Court was not a reasonable one and that the Trial Court had misread the evidence in convicting the accused. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. It is well settled that if two views are possible on the evidence adduced in a case of circumstantial evidence, the court should not disturb the finding of the trial court. [367B C] 2.1 When two views of the evidence are possible, the court has no option but to confirm the order of the acquittal. [368D E] 2.2 There is no justification for the invocation of the doctrine of benefit of doubt as against the decision of the trial judge who acquitted the accused. The view of the trial Judge acquitting an accused person cannot be said to have been reasonably connected with the crime he was charged at the time when he was tried and hence there could be no scope for invoking the doctrine of presumption. [369E F] 2.3 The view of acquittal recorded by the Sessions Judge was a plausible view and the High Court should not interfere with the same unless there were strong reasons which These principles apply equally to the appreciation of evidence in a criminal matter. [370F G] 3. The law requires that any view of the evidence in favour of the accused must be reasonable even as any one of those cases would be applicable where the guilt of the accused has been established beyond all reasonable doubts. [371A B] 4. The High Courts should not interfere in appeals against acquittals because they are not appellate authorities. [374G] 5. The High courts should not interfere at the instance of persons who are not before them when they act as such. [375H] 6. The High court should not interfere where the trial court has taken a possible view and has acquitted the accused merely because another view is also possible. [376A]
6778: The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court and Chief Justice of the High Court of Bombay was charged with an offence of criminal misconduct as defined in section 2(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was also charged under section 5 of the Act with the aid of section 6(1)(c) of the Act for having committed the offence of criminal mis conduct and dereliction of duty. The trial court convicted him but on appeal the High Court acquitted him holding that he had not been given the requisite sanction by the State Government. The High Court held that the sanction was invalid because it did not comply with the provisions of article 124(4) of the Constitution. The High court also held that the charge against the appellant was vague and no evidence could be led to prove his guilt. On appeal by special leave, the question for consideration was whether a Judge of a High Court can be prosecuted for an offence punishable under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the said Act except in the mode provided in article 124(5) of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) A Judge of the High Courts or of the High courts cannot be prosecuted and punished for an offence which does not fall within any of the clauses of article 124 of the Constitution unless it is established that he has been expressly authorised by the Constitution to do so. [764 D] (ii) It is well settled that if a person is accused of an offence involving moral turpitude, such offence is not to be taken cognizance of without there being a reasonable complaint in writing of the facts constituting such offence and the authority competent to remove the concerned judge from office. [765 H] (iii) In the present case, the High Court has not found that the appellant was guilty of any offence under section 5 or section 6 of the Act. [766 B] (iv) The charge against the accused was vague and did not disclose any specific allegation against him. [767 C]
2124: The appellant was a Sunri by caste. He filed an election petition claiming that he belonged to the Saha caste which had been recognised as a Scheduled Caste in West Bengal and that it was not open to him to claim that he belonged either to the Saha community or to any other caste. The High Court dismissed his petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a Sunri but a Sunri caste which had nothing to do with the Saha caste group within the Sunri caste group. [380 G] (ii) The appellant could not be said to belong to the Saha group because he did not belong to the Schedule Caste specified in item 40 of the Order. [381 D] (iii) There is no evidence on record to show that the appellant belonged to the Sahas. [382 B] (iv) The appellant 's case was that he belonged 'to the Saha caste, a smaller caste group within that very caste. The respondent had produced before the Tribunal the list of castes which were included in the Schedule to the Order. The appellant had also produced before the tribunal a copy of the list of the Saha caste. The appellant was therefore entitled to succeed. [383 C]

2052: The respondents were employed in banks which were not governed by the Sastry award as modified and were not thus drawing basic pay on the footing of scales of pay provided by that award. But the Government cannot take possession without resorting to a private individual who wants to take the land. [842A B]

2304: The appellant, a District and Sessions Judge, was transferred to the cadre of district judges. He challenged his transfer before the High Court on the ground that he had been arbitrarily transferred without any justification for the same. The High Court held that the power to transfer a district judge from one post to another was exclusively that of the Governor and not that of the Chief Justice and that the High Court had no authority to transfer him outside the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the High Court as such had no power to transfer him even though he held the post of a district judge in the cadre of District Judges; (ii) the High court had no power under article 233 to transfer a person holding a post outside the cadre of the High Court which was a State subject; and (iii) the High Courts power to appoint and transfer judges of High Courts is vested in the High Court and the Governor has no plenary power over them. HELD: (i) Article 235 does not confer upon the High Court the power to appoint or transfer a district Judge or a member of the service. [864 D] (ii)The High Court has power to transfer an officer who may be holding a post within its jurisdiction to another post outside its control. But the High Court cannot transfer a person who holds a post outside its jurisdiction to a post outside it. [865 C] (iii)It is true that the power of transfer is conferred by article 233 only on the Governor. But the power of appointment and promotion is vested in High Court. It is well settled that the power under article 235 is part of the administrative law of the country and the High Court has no inherent power to alter or modify the said law. [866 E F]

380: The appellants were displaced persons and the respondent entered into an agreement with them, whereby they leased out their mills to the appellants for a period of ten years. The lease was for a period not exceeding one year at a time but subject to certain terms and conditions. The appellants were put in possession of the mills on 31 8 1952. On 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants under section 10(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not be evicted. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the Custodian had no power to issue the notice under section 10 of the Act as he was not authorised by the Central Government to do so. The High Court held that the notice was invalid because it did not give any reasons for its action. Held, that the power conferred on the Custodian under section 12 of the Act is a judicial power and must be exercised within the four corners of the statute authorising him to do so, and that the Custodian has the power to cancel the lease or to take such other steps as he may consider necessary for carrying out the purposes of the Act. The power given to the Custodian under the Act is not an executive power, but a legislative power which can be delegated by the legislature under the guise of administration of justice to another body. The power of cancellation of leases granted by the evacuee is not an administrative power but a judicial power. The power to cancel leases granted by a person who is a party to a contract is not an essential element of his authority to enter into a contract. The Custodian has the right to decide whether a transaction is one of sale or mortgage. The power is discretionary and the discretion has to be exercised judicially and properly Would have been used in a proper case.

Section 6(2) empowered the Government by notification to exempt any class of persons from the operation of all or any of the provisions thereof. The Act did not impose any restrictions upon the traders in the matter of sale and purchase of agricultural produce. The Act, however, imposed a ban on the traders who were not registered dealers in respect of the agricultural produce sold in the notified market area. The Act also imposed a prohibition on the traders in certain specified areas in respect of transactions of sale and Purchase of agricultural produce outside the notified market. The Act provided for the establishment of a market committee

2256: The respondent was a thika tenant of the appellant in respect of certain lands. He filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he was a thikka tenant within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit given by him under section 3 of the Act as he was a tikkadar and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to his case. HELD: (i) The definition of a thika tenancy is wide enough to include a person who holds land from the thika tenant but does not include a person holding land from the Government or a local authority. [637 D] (ii) The expression 'thika tenant ' has been defined in section 2(5) of the Act to mean a tenant on direct purchase or under a tenant continuing in possession after the termination of his tenancy, but does not includes a person who held land from the government or a local body. [638 B C] (iii) The definition is wide enough so as to cover a person who occupies land from the land lord on the date of commencement of the Act. [639 E F]
